mcqs.question: A function has an `if/else` where a test only ever exercises the `if` branch. What does line coverage report for the untested `else` branch's line, if that line is reached by another test elsewhere in the same run?
options: It reports the else line as uncovered, since branch coverage subsumes line coverage
It will report the else line as covered if it executed at all, even though the false-path condition that leads there was never specifically exercised
It refuses to report a percentage until both branches are tested
Line coverage and branch coverage always report identical numbers
mcqs.explanation: Line coverage only asks whether a line executed, not which condition led there — so an else line executing via some other path still counts as covered under line coverage even if the specific branch condition was never tested. Branch coverage is the stricter metric that would catch this gap; the two are not identical.

mcqs.question: A test calls a function with two different inputs and asserts nothing about either return value, achieving 100% line and branch coverage. What does that prove about the function's correctness?
options: It proves the function handles both inputs correctly, since coverage tools verify output implicitly
It proves branch coverage is met but not line coverage
Nothing — coverage only measures that code executed, not that any result was checked
It proves the function is bug-free for those two specific inputs
mcqs.explanation: Coverage tools instrument execution, not assertions — a test with no assertion can hit 100% coverage while verifying nothing at all about correctness. Neither line nor branch coverage implies any checking happened, and the test proves nothing about whether the outputs were correct.

mcqs.question: A mutation testing tool flips a `>` to `>=` in your source code and reruns your test suite. Every test still passes. What does that outcome, on its own, indicate?
options: The mutant was killed, proving your tests are thorough
The mutation testing tool has a bug and should be re-run
Your code has no bugs related to that comparison
The mutant survived — no test in your suite would have caught this specific bug if it existed in your real code
mcqs.explanation: A surviving mutant means the suite ran unchanged despite a real behavioral change to the code, which is direct evidence that a bug in that exact shape would ship undetected. A kill requires at least one test to go red, and a survival says nothing about whether the tool is broken or the original code is bug-free.

mcqs.question: A team's coverage percentage drops by two points after a refactor. Treating coverage strictly as a diagnostic rather than a target, what's the appropriate first reaction?
options: Immediately block the merge until coverage is restored to its prior number
Ignore it — coverage percentage changes are never meaningful
Investigate what specifically became uncovered and whether that gap is a real risk, rather than treating the drop itself as the problem
Add assertion-free tests to the uncovered lines to restore the percentage quickly
mcqs.explanation: Treating coverage as a diagnostic means using a drop as a prompt to investigate the specific gap, not as an automatic failure condition — the drop might be harmless (removed dead code) or a real risk, and only looking at what changed tells you which. Blocking on the raw number or patching with hollow tests are exactly the target-chasing behaviors this framing avoids.

mcqs.question: A CI pipeline blocks merges below 80% coverage. Engineers under deadline pressure start writing tests that call every new function without asserting on results, and the gate passes. What has actually happened to the team's bug-catching ability?
options: It has improved, since more code paths are now exercised during tests
It hasn't necessarily improved, and may be worse, because the new tests create an illusion of safety that an honest gap would not
It is unaffected either way, since coverage gates don't influence code quality
It is impossible to write a test that raises coverage without adding real verification
mcqs.explanation: Assertion-free tests raise the percentage without adding any real bug-catching power, and worse, they can mislead a team into believing coverage there than an honest zero-coverage gap would — which at least is visibly untested. It's straightforward to write exactly this kind of hollow test, and the gate being satisfied says nothing about actual quality improving.

mcqs.question: A team wants a coverage policy that targets new risk without demanding retroactive tests for years-old legacy code. Which approach fits best?
options: Gate pull requests on diff coverage — new or changed lines must be covered — rather than a single global percentage threshold
Require 100% global coverage before any new feature can be merged
Remove all coverage tooling since legacy code makes any threshold unfair
Only measure coverage on the legacy code, since new code is assumed to be tested by convention
mcqs.explanation: Diff coverage targets exactly the risk that matters — new or changed code — without punishing a codebase for legacy files that have run safely for years without full coverage. A 100% global requirement or measuring only legacy code both misplace the target, and dropping tooling entirely throws away the diagnostic value coverage does have.
